rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of Paradise trade worldly life for the afterlife, while the people of the Fire trade the afterlife for worldly life; this is figurative exchange and loss.
rows.anchor: أهل الجنة اشتروا الآخرة بترك الدنيا، واشترى أهل النار الدنيا بترك الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God divided people between Paradise and Fire and assigned everyone a dwelling in both; the guided may inherit the place of the forsaken, producing the ultimate exchange.
rows.anchor: فريقا للجنة وفريقا للنار. ومنازل الكل موضوعة في الجنة والنار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This exchange may also be described as inheritance, as explained under the opening of al-Mu’minun.
rows.anchor: وقد يخبر عن هذا التبادل بالوراثة كما بيناه في قد أفلح المؤمنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Loss can occur before Judgment, but this verse concerns the final loss whose consequences cannot be repaired.
rows.anchor: ولكنه أراد التغابن الذين لا جبران لنهايته

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: They report three losses: discarded knowledge later practiced by a student, ill-gotten wealth wisely used by an heir, and an obedient slave saved while his sinful master is ruined.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة: بلغنا أن التغابن في ثلاثة أصناف

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report describes a husband condemned for unlawful earnings and neglecting support, while his wife is admitted to Paradise and tells him their fates have been exchanged.
rows.anchor: فيقول الله تعالى قد صدقت فيؤمر به إلى النار ويؤمر بها إلى الجنة

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says the verse’s restriction of mutual loss to Judgment Day proves worldly transaction loss is impermissible; the Baghdadis would rescind a sale when the loss exceeds one-third.
rows.anchor: على أنه لا يجوز الغبن في المعاملة الدنيوية

rows.speaker: البغداديون
rows.claim: The Baghdadi jurists support rescission for substantial loss with the Prophet’s instruction to Hibbān ibn Munqidh to disclaim fraud and retain a three-day option.
rows.anchor: إذا بايعت فقل لا خلابة ولك الخيار ثلاثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says fraud is religiously forbidden by consensus, but slight loss cannot be avoided; substantial avoidable loss warrants rescission, with one-third set by analogy to bequests.
rows.anchor: لكن اليسير منه لايمكن الاحتراز عنه لأحد، فمضى في البيوع إذ لو حكمنا برده ما نفذ بيع أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the verse to mean that unrestricted loss is permitted only on that Day.
rows.anchor: ذلك يوم التغابن الجائز مطلقا من غير تفصيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it means irreparable loss: worldly losses may be reversed or offset by later profit, whereas losing Paradise can never be recovered.
rows.anchor: فأما من خسر الجنة فلا درك له أبدا

rows.speaker: بعض علماء الصوفية
rows.claim: Some Sufi scholars say everyone meets God at a loss because no one can fully perform enough works to receive complete recompense.
rows.anchor: إن الله كتب الغبن على الخلق أجمعين، فلا يلقى أحد ربه إلا مغبونا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says everyone meets God regretful: the wrongdoer regrets failing to do good, and the good-doer regrets failing to do more.
rows.anchor: لا يلقى الله أحد إلا نادما إن كان مسيئا إن لم يحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafi and Ibn Amir read both verbs in the first-person plural; the other readers use the third-person form.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وابن عامر بالنون فيهما، والباقون بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A husband supports his wife and young child according to his means; a well-off provider gives more, while a poor one gives what he can.
rows.anchor: لينفق الزوج على زوجته وعلى ولده الصغير على قدر وسعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Under the author’s view, a judge or mufti estimates support from both the recipient’s need and the provider’s means, guided by customary living standards.
rows.anchor: فتقدر النفقة بحسب الحالة من المنفق والحاجة من المنفق عليه بالاجتهاد

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأصحابه
rows.claim: Shafi‘i and his companions hold that maintenance is fixed solely by the husband’s means, without regard to the wife’s means or sufficiency; they prescribe two, one-and-a-half, or one mudd.
rows.anchor: النفقة مقدرة محددة، ولا اجتهاد لحاكم ولا لمفت فيها

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأصحابه
rows.claim: They argue that measuring support by need is unknowable and invites disputes, so a caliph’s daughter and a guard’s daughter receive the same amount.
rows.anchor: فيجب لابنة الخليفة ما يجب لابنة الحارس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi answers that the verse establishes differences between rich and poor husbands but does not exclude the wife’s condition from customary support.
rows.anchor: فأما إنه لا اعتبار بحال الزوجة على وجهه فليس فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to provide according to recognized custom applies to both spouses; customary support for a wealthy woman is not the same as for a poor woman.
rows.anchor: وذلك يقتضي تعلق المعروف في حقهما لأنه لم يخص في ذلك واحدا منهما

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet told Hind to take what adequately supported her and her child according to custom.
rows.anchor: خذي ما يكفيك وولدك بالمعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet referred Hind to what sufficed her, based on Abu Sufyan’s means, rather than imposing a fixed amount; the verse itself does not establish fixed rates.
rows.anchor: فأحالها على الكفاية حين علم السعة من حال أبي سفيان

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar assigned a newborn a monthly allowance of one hundred dirhams, while Uthman assigned fifty; Ibn al-Arabi suggests prices or circumstances may explain the difference.
rows.anchor: روي أن عمر رضي الله عنه فرض للمنفوس مائة درهم، وفرض له عثمان خمسين درهما

rows.speaker: محمد بن هلال المزني
rows.claim: He reports from his father and grandmother that Uthman sent a newborn fifty dirhams and a garment, promising to raise the grant to one hundred after a year.
rows.anchor: ولدت الليلة فبعث إليها بخمسين درهما وشقيقة سنبلانية

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali assigned a foundling an allowance of one hundred dirhams.
rows.anchor: وقد أتي علي رضي الله عنه بمنبوذ ففرض له مائة

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says scholars differ whether support before weaning is recommended or obligatory; he holds it obligatory and says its amount varies with circumstances at birth and weaning.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من رآه واجبا لما تجدد من حاجته وعرض من مؤونته وبه أقول

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Sufyan ibn Wahb reports that Umar set each Muslim a monthly ration of two mudd of wheat and one qist each of vinegar and oil.
rows.anchor: إني فرضت لكل نفس مسلمة في كل شهر مدي حنطة وقسطي خل وقسطي زيت

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Abu al-Darda praises the practices Umar established for Muhammad’s community as rightly guided.
rows.anchor: كم سنة راشدة مهدية قد سنها عمر رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Syrian mudd and qist measures have changed; support includes customary food and clothing, adjusted to circumstances and local custom.
rows.anchor: وأما الكسوة فبقدر العادة قميص وسراويل وجبة في الشتاء وكساء وإزار وحصير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes that a father, rather than the mother, must support a child.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية أصل في وجوب النفقة للولد على الوالد دون الأم

rows.speaker: محمد بن المواز
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn al-Mawwaz says both parents owe child support in proportion to their inheritance shares; Ibn al-Arabi suggests he may mean the mother only when no father exists.
rows.anchor: إنها على الأبوين على قدر الميراث

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report lists a wife, an enslaved worker, and a child each asking the addressee to provide for them, with the child asking who else will support him.
rows.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an and Sunnah reinforce the same rule about a person’s responsibility to provide for dependents.
rows.anchor: فقد تعاضد القرآن والسنة وتواردا في شرعة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not charge a poor person as He charges a wealthy one; hardship is followed by wealth and greater ease.
rows.anchor: أي لا يكلف الفقير مثل ما يكلف الغني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable addresses Meccans: wealth was a test meant to elicit gratitude, but their arrogance and hostility to Muhammad were followed by famine and drought.
rows.anchor: أعطيناهم أموالا ليشكروا لا ليبطروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden story was locally known: a Yemenite owner gave God’s due, but after his death his sons withheld it and God destroyed the orchard.
rows.anchor: وكانت لرجل يؤدي حق الله تعالى منها فلما مات صارت إلى ولده، فمنعوا الناس خيرها

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi locates the garden two farsakhs from Sanaa and says God burned it.
rows.anchor: كان بينهم وبين صنعاء فرسخان ابتلاهم الله بأن أحرق جنتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account places the garden at Dawran, one farsakh from Sanaa, and says its owners were miserly after Jesus was raised.
rows.anchor: هي جنة بضوران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says the owners harvested at night to keep the poor away; at dawn they found the garden uprooted and blackened.
rows.anchor: وكانوا بخلاء فكانوا يجدون التمر ليلا من أجل المساكين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: If al-sarim means night, the garden was blackened; if it means day, its trees and crops had vanished and the soil was bare.
rows.anchor: فإن كان أراد الليل فلاسوداد موضعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One account says Gabriel swept the garden away, circled it around the Kaaba, and placed it where Taif now stands, explaining its name and fertility.
rows.anchor: وكان الطائف الذي طاف عليها جبريل عليه السلام فاقتلعها

rows.speaker: البكري
rows.claim: Al-Bakri instead derives Taif’s name from a man of Sadaf who built a wall around the town.
rows.anchor: سميت الطائف لأن رجلا من الصدف يقال له الدمون، بنى حائطا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says harvesters should share crops with poor people present, based on 6:141; the right is distinct from zakat, and he prefers the view that night harvesting was prohibited to avoid depriving them.
rows.anchor: وإنما قلنا الأول أصح لأن العقوبة كانت بسبب ما أرادوه من منع المساكين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a righteous owner had three sons and gave the poor all fallen grapes, missed fruit, stray grain, and spilled threshed produce.
rows.anchor: كانت تلك الجنة دون صنعاء بفرسخين، غرسها رجل من أهل الصلاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father’s charity supported orphans, widows, and poor people; after he died, the sons complained of fewer assets and more dependents.
rows.anchor: وكان يعيش في ذلك في حياة أبيهم اليتامى والأرامل والمساكين، فلما مات أبوهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sons agreed to go before the poor at dawn and secretly harvest the garden so the needy would not know.
rows.anchor: فتحالفوا بينهم ليغدون غدوة قبل خروج الناس ثم ليصرمنها ولا تعرف المساكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They meant to cut the date clusters at dawn under night’s dimness; sarm means cutting, and asrama means that the palms are ready to harvest.
rows.anchor: ليقطعن ثمر نخيلهم إذا أصبحوا بسدفة من الليل لئلا ينتبه المساكين لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They made no exception” means they did not say “if God wills.”
rows.anchor: أي ولم يقولوا إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sons called one another at daybreak to set out and harvest; the verb means that one person called another.
rows.anchor: { فتنادوا مصبحين } ينادي بعضهم بعضا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains “your harvest” as the crop they planned to reap.
rows.anchor: حاصدين زرعكم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says their harvest was grapes, and they did not say “if God wills.”
rows.anchor: كان حرثهم عنبا ولم يقولوا إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih says their formula of exception was “Glory be to God, our Lord.”
rows.anchor: كان استثناؤهم قولهم سبحان الله

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima interprets their failure to make an exception as failing to exempt the poor’s due from their plan.
rows.anchor: أي لا يستثنون حق المساكين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the destructive visitor was a command from God; Qatada calls it punishment, and Ibn Jurayj describes a fiery neck from Hell’s valley.
rows.anchor: أمر من ربك. وقال قتادة: عذاب من ربك

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says a ta’if, or night visitor, comes only at night.
rows.anchor: والطائف لا يكون إلا بالليل قاله الفراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says people can be held accountable for a firm intention: the garden owners were punished before carrying out their plan, as in the threat concerning wrongdoing in the Sacred Mosque.
rows.anchor: ومن يرد فيه بإلحاد بظلم نذقه من عذاب أليم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A sound report says both combatants who meet with swords are in Hell, including the victim because he was eager to kill his opponent.
rows.anchor: إذا التقى المسلمان بسيفيهما فالقاتل والمقتول في النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi also points to the discussion under the verse about those who do not persist in wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: ولم يصروا على ما فعلوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والفراء
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Farra, and others explain al-sarim as a dark night; the scorched garden became black like night.
rows.anchor: أي كالليل المظلم عن ابن عباس والفراء وغيرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poem describes the dark night as long and unable to clear by dawn, illustrating the night sense of al-sarim.
rows.anchor: تطاول ليلك الجون البهيم فما ينجاب عن صبح بهيم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also says al-sarim means black ash, using a Khuzaymi dialect word.
rows.anchor: الصريم الرماد الأسود بلغة خزيمة

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: Al-Thawri says it means a harvested crop, with al-sarim understood as something cut down.
rows.anchor: كالزرع المحصود. فالصريم بمعنى المصروم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan explains that its good was cut off, treating al-sarim as a passive form.
rows.anchor: صرم عنها الخير أي قطع فالصريم مفعول أيضا

rows.speaker: المؤرج
rows.claim: Al-Mu’arrij compares it to a patch of sand separated from a larger dune, where nothing useful grows.
rows.anchor: الرملة لا تنبت شيئا ينتفع به.

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash says al-sarim is the morning separated from night.
rows.anchor: كالصبح انصرم من الليل

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad interprets it as daytime, when nothing remains in the garden.
rows.anchor: كالنهار فلا شيء فيها

rows.speaker: شمر
rows.claim: Shammir says both night and day are called sarim because each separates from the other; one view derives the night name from darkness stopping activity.
rows.anchor: الصريم الليل والصريم النهار أي ينصرم هذا عن ذاك وذاك عن هذا

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri objects that night cannot be called sarim because it stops activity, since day is also called sarim.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا نظر لأن النهار يسمى صريما ولا يقطع عن تصرف

rows.speaker: عطاء وقتادة
rows.claim: Ata and Qatada say the brothers whispered and concealed their speech so no one would learn of their plan.
rows.anchor: قاله عطاء وقتادة. وهو من خفت يخفت إذا سكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb may mean they hid themselves from people, since their father used to alert the poor to come at harvest time.
rows.anchor: يخفون أنفسهم من الناس حتى لا يروهم. وكان أبوهم يخبر الفقراء

rows.speaker: دريد بن الصمة
rows.claim: Duraid ibn al-Simma’s verse is cited as evidence for the word khufatan, a quiet or secret manner.
rows.anchor: وإني لم أهلك سلالا ولم أمت خفاتا وكلا ظنه بي عودي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others explain hard as intention and say the brothers believed they had the ability to carry out their purpose.
rows.anchor: أي على قصد وقدرة في أنفسهم ويظنون أنهم تمكنوا من مرادهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hard means purpose or intention, as in the expression “I intended your intention.”
rows.anchor: والحرد القصد. حرد يحرد بالكسر حردا قصد.

rows.speaker: الشاعر الراجز
rows.claim: A rajaz line compares the brothers’ directed purpose to a flood heading for a fruitful garden; al-Mubarrad says the garden bears produce, while others describe water flowing through its furrows.
rows.anchor: أقبل سيل جاء من عند الله يحرد حرد الجنة المغله

rows.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد
rows.claim: Qatada and Mujahid gloss hard as earnest effort.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة ومجاهد: «على حرد» أي على جد. الحسن: على حاجة وفاقة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says it means they were in need and poverty.
rows.anchor: الحسن: على حاجة وفاقة. وقال أبو عبيدة والقتيبي:

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والقتيبي
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda and al-Qutaybi say hard means withholding, from the term for camels whose milk has dwindled.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة والقتيبي: على حرد على منع من قولهم حاردت الإبل حرادا

rows.speaker: السدي وسفيان
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Sufyan interpret hard as anger.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي وسفيان: { على حرد } على غضب. والحرد الغضب

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit says hard may be vocalized with a fatḥa and describes an angry lion; a verse also uses it for anger.
rows.anchor: تقول منه: حرد بالكسر حردا، فهو حارد وحردان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is isolation: hard means withdrawing from one’s people; Hudhayl uses munḥarid for solitary, and al-Azhari says Hard was their village’s name.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «على حرد» على انفراد. يقال: حرد يحرد حرودا أي تنحى عن قومه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Hard was the name of their garden; the word has two pronunciations.
rows.anchor: اسم جنتهم وفيه لغتان: حرد وحرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers have the word with a quiescent letter; Abu al-Aliya and Ibn al-Sumayqa read it with fatḥa, both being dialectal forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ العامة بالإسكان. وقرأ أبو العالية وابن السميقع بالفتح

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says qadirin means they had planned and determined their affair.
rows.anchor: قد قدروا أمرهم وبنوا عليه قاله الفراء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says they considered themselves able to control their garden.
rows.anchor: قادرين على جنتهم عند أنفسهم

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha‘bi says they thought they were able to keep the poor away.
rows.anchor: «قادرين» يعني على المساكين. وقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that they had the means to withhold charity but chose to do so.
rows.anchor: معناه من الوجود أي منعوا وهم واجدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing the burnt, blackened garden, the brothers failed to recognize it and wondered whether they had lost their way.
rows.anchor: قد صارت كالليل الأسود ينظرون إليها كالرماد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets their words as saying that they had taken the wrong road to their garden.
rows.anchor: أي ضللنا الطريق إلى جنتنا قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, they recognized their wrongful dawn plan to exclude the poor and understood the destruction as punishment.
rows.anchor: إنا لضالون عن الصواب في غدونا على نية منع المساكين فلذلك عوقبنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They conclude that they have been deprived of their garden because of what they did.
rows.anchor: أي حرمنا جنتنا بما صنعنا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Masud warns that sin may deprive someone of provision prepared for him, and the Prophet recites the garden passage.
rows.anchor: إياكم والمعاصي إن العبد ليذنب الذنب فيحرم به رزقا كان هيىء له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their middle brother was the most excellent, just, and intelligent among them.
rows.anchor: أي أمثلهم وأعدلهم وأعقلهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and others understand “why do you not glorify?” as “why do you not make an exception by saying if God wills”; the brother had warned them, but they ignored him.
rows.anchor: وهذا يدل على أن هذا الأوسط كان أمرهم بالاستثناء فلم يطيعوه

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih says their exception was “Glory be to God”; the brother asks why they did not praise God and thank Him for what He gave them.
rows.anchor: فقال لهم: هلا تسبحون الله أي تقولون سبحان الله

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas says tasbih is declaring God transcendent; Mujahid’s reading works because it denies that anything happens except by God’s will.
rows.anchor: لأن المعنى تنزيه الله عز وجل أن يكون شيء إلا بمشيئته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that the brother urged them to seek forgiveness and repent their corrupt intention, recalling God’s punishment of wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: هلا تستغفرونه من فعلكم وتتوبون إليه من خبث نيتكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says their declaration of God’s glory means they sought forgiveness for their sin; they admit they wronged themselves by denying the poor.
rows.anchor: أي نستغفر الله من ذنبنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers blamed one another over the oath and exclusion of the poor, each accusing another of proposing the plan.
rows.anchor: بل أنت أشرت علينا بهذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They call themselves transgressors for disobeying God by withholding the poor’s right and failing to make an exception.
rows.anchor: أي عاصين بمنع حق الفقراء وترك الاستثناء

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan says they transgressed God’s blessings by failing to thank Him as their fathers had.
rows.anchor: طغينا نعم الله فلم نشكرها كما شكرها آباؤنا من قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They pledged to act like their fathers if God replaced the garden, prayed and repented, and God replaced it that night; Gabriel moved the old garden to Syria and brought another in its place.
rows.anchor: وقالوا: إن أبدلنا الله خيرا منها لنصنعن

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says God recognized their sincerity and gave them a garden called al-Hayawan, whose grape cluster could be carried by a mule.
rows.anchor: إن القوم أخلصوا وعرف الله منهم صدقهم فأبدلهم جنة

rows.speaker: اليماني أبو خالد
rows.claim: Abu Khalid says he saw the replacement garden, whose grape clusters were each like a standing dark-skinned man.
rows.anchor: دخلت تلك الجنة فرأيت كل عنقود منها كالرجل الأسود القائم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan is unsure whether their final longing for God was genuine faith or the distress-driven words of polytheists, so their faith remains uncertain.
rows.anchor: لا أدري إيمانا كان ذلك منهم، أو على حد ما يكون من المشركين إذا أصابتهم الشدة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: When asked whether the garden owners were destined for Paradise or Hell, Qatada said the question had burdened him.
rows.anchor: لقد كلفتني تعبا

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Most scholars say the owners repented sincerely; al-Qushayri transmits this view.
rows.anchor: إنهم تابوا وأخلصوا حكاه القشيري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the light form yubaddilana; readers of Medina and Abu Amr double the consonant, both being valid forms.
rows.anchor: بالتخفيف. وقرأ أهل المدينة وأبو عمرو بالتشديد، وهما لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabdil can change a thing or its state while the object remains, whereas ibdal removes one thing and puts another in its place.
rows.anchor: التبديل تغيير الشيء أو تغيير حاله وعين الشيء قائم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak identifies the human created as halu‘ as a disbeliever.
rows.anchor: يعني الكافر، عن الضحاك

rows.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد
rows.claim: Halu‘ linguistically means extreme greed and the worst, most excessive panic; the intensified form describes a person impatient in good and hardship.
rows.anchor: أشد الحرص وأسوأ الجزع وأفحشه

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima defines halu‘ as fretful and distressed.
rows.anchor: عكرمة: هو الضجور. الضحاك: هو الذي لا يشبع

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the halu‘ person is never satiated.
rows.anchor: الضحاك: هو الذي لا يشبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The miserly person is one who receives wealth but withholds God’s due from it.
rows.anchor: هو الذي إذا أصاب المال منع منه حق الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan says people love what pleases them and flee what displeases them, yet God commands them to spend what they love and endure what they dislike.
rows.anchor: ثم تعبده الله بإنفاق ما يحب والصبر على ما يكره

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda, as transmitted by Tha‘lab, defines halu‘ as failing to give thanks when blessed and failing to endure harm.
rows.anchor: هو الذي إذا مسه الخير لم يشكر، وإذا مسه الضر لم يصبر، قاله ثعلب

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Tha‘lab also reads the following verses as defining halu‘: extreme distress when harmed and withholding good from people when prosperous.
rows.anchor: إذا ناله الشر أظهر شدة الجزع، وإذا ناله الخير بخل به ومنعه الناس

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A prophetic saying calls grasping greed and destabilizing cowardice the worst gifts given to a servant.
rows.anchor: شر ما أعطي العبد شح هالع وجبن خالع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab usage also calls a fast-moving, light-footed she-camel halwa‘a or halwa‘; a cited line witnesses to that word.
rows.anchor: ناقة هلواعة وهلواع إذا كانت سريعة السير خفيفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Jazu‘an” and “manu‘an” are adjectives for halu‘, understood as moved forward before the following conditional, or as the predicate of an implied kana.
rows.anchor: نعتان لهلوع. على أن ينوي بهما التقديم قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception of those who pray shows that the preceding human traits concern disbelievers; “human” is generic, like the general statement and exception in al-Asr.
rows.anchor: دل على أن ما قبله في الكفار، فالإنسان اسم جنس بدليل الاستثناء الذي يعقبه

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakha‘i identifies those who pray as people who perform the obligatory prayer.
rows.anchor: المراد بالمصلين الذين يؤدون الصلاة المكتوبة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says they observe prayer at its prescribed time, and abandoning prayer is unbelief.
rows.anchor: الذين يصلونها لوقتها، فأما تركها فكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations identify them as the Companions or believers generally, who overcome panic through trust in God and certainty.
rows.anchor: هم الصحابة. وقيل: هم المؤمنون عامة، فإنهم يغلبون فرط الجزع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being constant in prayer means observing its appointed times; ‘constant’ also means still, as in the ban on urinating in still water.
rows.anchor: نهي عن البول في الماء الدائم

rows.speaker: عقبة بن عامر
rows.claim: Uqba ibn Amir says the constant worshippers do not turn right or left while praying.
rows.anchor: هم الذين إذا صلوا لم يلتفتوا يمينا ولا شمالا

rows.speaker: ابن جريج والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj and Hasan interpret constancy as frequently performing voluntary prayers.
rows.anchor: هم الذين يكثرون فعل التطوع منها

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن سيرين
rows.claim: Qatada and Ibn Sirin identify the known, specified right in wealth as obligatory zakat.
rows.anchor: يريد الزكاة المفروضة، قاله قتادة وابن سيرين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the specified right is an obligation beyond zakat.
rows.anchor: سوى الزكاة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the right as maintaining kinship ties and bearing burdens for others.
rows.anchor: صلة رحم وحمل كل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi prefers zakat because it is a known amount, while additional giving varies with the recipient’s need.
rows.anchor: والأول أصح، لأنه وصف الحق بأنه معلوم، وسوى الزكاة ليس بمعلوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanation of the petitioner and deprived person was given earlier in al-Dhariyat.
rows.anchor: تقدم في «الذاريات». { والذين يصدقون بيوم الدين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believing in the Day of Judgment means believing in Resurrection and recompense, discussed under al-Fatiha.
rows.anchor: أي بيوم الجزاء وهو يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says punishment is especially not safe for those who associate partners with God or deny His messengers; another view says everyone must fear it.
rows.anchor: لمن أشرك أو كذب أنبياءه. وقيل: لا يأمنه أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanation of guarding sexual chastity except with spouses or owned women was given under al-Mu’minun.
rows.anchor: تقدم القول فيه في سورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanation of keeping trusts and covenants was already given under the earlier passage in al-Mu’minun.
rows.anchor: والذين هم لأماناتهم وعهدهم راعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They give testimony for anyone, near or distant, before a judge without concealing or altering it; the legal discussion is under al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: يقومون بها عند الحاكم ولا يكتمونها ولا يغيرونها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says their testimony is that God is one without partner and Muhammad is His servant and messenger.
rows.anchor: أن الله واحد لا شريك له وأن محمدا عبده ورسوله

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read ‘trusts’ in the singular; it is a generic noun encompassing religious duties and people’s deposits.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة ابن كثير وابن محيصن. فالأمانة اسم جنس

rows.speaker: عباس الدوري عن أبي عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: Al-Duri from Abu Amr and Yaqub read ‘testimonies’ in the plural; the other readers use the singular, which can represent a group as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عباس الدوري عن أبي عمرو ويعقوب { بشهاداتهم } جمعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one can shield the Prophet from God’s punishment if he seeks refuge in them; his opponents had offered to protect him if he abandoned his message.
rows.anchor: لا يدفع عذابه عني أحد إن استحفظته وهذا لأنهم قالوا اترك ما تدعو إليه

rows.speaker: أبو الجوزاء عن ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud recounts accompanying the Prophet to al-Hajun on the night of the jinn; their leader Wardan offered to repel them, and the Prophet answered that no one could protect him from God.
rows.anchor: فقال سيدهم يقال له وردان: أنا أزجلهم عنك

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi offers two readings: no one can protect him alongside God’s protection, or no one can protect him from what God decrees.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل معنيين أحدهما لن يجيرني مع إجارة الله لي أحد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says multahad means a refuge; he also glosses it as helper or patron.
rows.anchor: أي ملتجأ ألجأ إليه قاله قتادة. وعنه: نصيرا ومولى

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi interprets multahad as a fortress.
rows.anchor: السدي: حرزا

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says it means an underground entrance or burrow in which one might hide.
rows.anchor: الكلبي: مدخلا في الأرض مثل السرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views gloss it as a guardian, patron, place to turn, or path; the meanings converge, and a line of poetry uses the word for refuge from divine decree.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وليا ولا مولى. وقيل مذهبا ولا مسلكا

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ankal means chains or restraints; its singular nakal prevents movement, and one explanation says it is named for making an example of its bearer.
rows.anchor: الأنكال: القيود. عن الحسن ومجاهد وغيرهما. واحدها نكل، وهو ما منع الإنسان

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha‘bi says the chains are not needed to stop escape: when the people of Hell try to rise, they slip back down.
rows.anchor: أترون أن الله تعالى جعل الأنكال في أرجل أهل النار خشية أن يهربوا

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies ankal as shackles.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: الأنكال: الأغلال

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil interprets the term as kinds of severe punishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه أنواع العذاب الشديد قاله مقاتل

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report defines the phrase “nukl upon nukl” as a strong, experienced man riding a strong, experienced horse; the word can signify a powerful restraint or punishment.
rows.anchor: إن الله يحب النكل على النكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jahim is the raging, kindled Fire.
rows.anchor: والجحيم النار المؤججة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The choking food is unswallowable and may be ghislin, zaqqum, or dari‘; Ibn Abbas also says it is a thorn lodged in the throat, neither passing down nor coming out.
rows.anchor: وهو الغسلين والزقوم والضريع قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj identifies the food as dari‘, citing the statement that they have no food except dari‘; it is a thorn like osage orange.
rows.anchor: أي طعامهم الضريع كما قال: ليس لهم طعام إلا من ضريع

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the food as zaqqum, citing the verse that calls the tree the food of the sinner; Qurtubi says the interpretations converge.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هو الزقوم، كما قال

rows.speaker: حمران بن أعين
rows.claim: Hamran ibn A‘yan reports that the Prophet recited the verses about chains, fire, and choking food, then fainted.
rows.anchor: وطعاما ذا غصة } فصعق

rows.speaker: خليد بن حسان
rows.claim: Khalid ibn Hassan recounts that Hasan repeatedly refused food after these verses were recited, finally taking a sip of sawiq after visitors urged him.
rows.anchor: فجاؤوه فلم يزالوا به حتى شرب شربة من سويق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghussa means a morsel, bone, or other thing caught in the throat; the passage also explains its plural, related forms, and the expression for a crowded house.
rows.anchor: والغصة: الشجا، وهو ما ينشب في الحلق من عظم أو غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word yawm may be an adverb for when they are punished, may follow an omitted preposition, or may depend on “leave Me and the deniers.”
rows.anchor: وانتصب «يوم» على الظرف أي ينكل بهم

rows.speaker: الضحاك والكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi say a heaped sand mass is mahil because it slides underfoot and collapses when its base is removed.
rows.anchor: المهيل: هو الذي إذا وطئته بالقدم زل من تحتها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains mahil as loose, flowing sand scattered about.
rows.anchor: «مهيلا» أي رملا سائلا متناثرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mahil is the passive form of “I poured dust”; the text gives parallel forms and a poetic example for the pattern.
rows.anchor: هلت عليه التراب أهيله هيلا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When people complained of poor harvests, the Prophet asked whether they measured or poured grain loose; he told them to measure it for blessing.
rows.anchor: كيلوا طعامكم يبارك لكم فيه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra treats kalla as an added particle attached to the oath, understood as “by the moon.”
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: «كلا» صلة للقسم، التقدير أي والقمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading takes kalla to mean “truly”; on either reading there is no pause after it.
rows.anchor: المعنى حقا والقمر فلا يوقف على هذين التقديرين

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari permits a pause after kalla and reads it as rejecting the claim that people can resist Hell’s keepers before the oath begins.
rows.anchor: وجعلها ردا للذين زعموا أنهم يقاومون خزنة جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafi, Hamza, and Hafs read “when the night turned away” with idh; other readers use idha, and some read dabbara without the prefix, forms treated as synonyms by al-Farra and al-Akhfash.
rows.anchor: «إذ أدبر» الباقون «إذا» بألف و «دبر» بغير ألف وهما لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some linguists distinguish dabbara, when night has passed, from adbára, when it begins to withdraw.
rows.anchor: دبر الليل: إذا مضى، وأدبر: أخذ في الإدبار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: When Mujahid asked about idha dabbara, Ibn Abbas waited until night had passed and then said it was that moment.
rows.anchor: فسكت حتى إذا دبر قال: يا مجاهد، هذا حين دبر الليل

rows.speaker: محمد بن السميقع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sumayqa reads the phrase with two alifs; the same form appears in the codices attributed to Abd Allah and Ubayy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ محمد بن السميقع { والليل إذ أدبر } بألفين

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub says readers of dabbara mean that night approaches from behind; Abu Amr calls it a Qurayshi usage.
rows.anchor: من قول العرب دبر فلان: إذا جاء من خلفي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In another report Ibn Abbas says adbára is correct, since a camel’s back is described as dabbara.
rows.anchor: الصواب: «أدبر» إنما يدبر ظهر البعير

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd prefers idha adbára because it matches the following idha asfara; he says Quranic oaths are followed by idha rather than idh.
rows.anchor: لأنها أكثر موافقة للحروف التي تليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asfara means that morning light brightened; the common reading has the alif, while Ibn al-Sumayqa reads safara, another dialectal form.
rows.anchor: ومعنى «أسفر»: ضاء. وقراءة العامة

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet’s instruction to delay the dawn prayer until it brightens is explained as praying after the light appears or lengthening prayer until sunrise approaches.
rows.anchor: أسفروا بالفجر، فإنه أعظم للأجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word may describe a face shining or a woman uncovering her face; it may also derive from sweeping away darkness, as a broom clears a house.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون من سفر الظلام أي كنسه، كما يسفر البيت أي يكنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath’s answer says this Fire is one of the great calamities; Muqatil says al-kubar is a name of Hell, while Ibn Abbas reports denial of Muhammad or the Hour as alternatives.
rows.anchor: جواب القسم أي إن هذه النار

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says al-kubar is one of Hell’s names.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير مقاتل «الكبر»: اسم من أسماء النار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also interprets “it” as the denial of Muhammad, a great sin, or as the rising of the Hour.
rows.anchor: إن قيام الساعة لإحدى الكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-kubar means the great and severe punishments; the cited rajaz verse uses kubar for a major calamity.
rows.anchor: والكبر: هي العظائم من العقوبات

rows.speaker: جرير بن حازم عن ابن كثير
rows.claim: The common reading is la-ihda with a hamza, while Ibn Kathir is reported to read la-hda without it.
rows.anchor: وروى جرير بن حازم عن ابن كثير «إنها لحدى الكبر» بحذف الهمزة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says nadhiran means the Fire is a warning to humanity, functioning as a circumstantial accusative; masculine form reflects its meaning as punishment or as “possessing warning.”
rows.anchor: نصب على الحال من المضمر

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil treats nadhir as a verbal noun like nakir, which explains its use for a feminine referent.
rows.anchor: النذير: مصدر كالنكير، ولذلك يوصف به المؤنث

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says creation has never been warned of anything more terrifying than the Fire.
rows.anchor: والله ما أنذر الخلائق بشيء أدهى منها

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي وابن زيد
rows.claim: They interpret the warner as Muhammad, resuming the command at the start of the sura to rise and warn; this is also reported from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: المراد بالنذير محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم أي قم نذيرا للبشر

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra rejects attaching nadhiran to the opening command because too much text intervenes; another report says this syntax is awkward for the same reason.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض المفسرين معناه «يأيها المدثر قم نذيرا للبشر»

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: Abu Razin says God Himself is the warner, telling people to fear the Fire.
rows.anchor: أنا لكم منها نذير فاتقوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other syntactic proposals make nadhiran a circumstantial phrase referring to the one who knows God’s forces, or a verbal noun meaning warning; it may also modify an implied verb.
rows.anchor: هو حال من «هو» في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Abla reads nadhir in the nominative, supplying an implied “it is.”
rows.anchor: «نذير» بالرفع، على إضمار هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes the Quran itself the warning because it contains promises and threats.
rows.anchor: إن القرآن نذير للبشر، لما تضمنه من الوعد والوعيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase is linked to nadhiran: it warns whoever chooses to advance toward good and obedience or fall behind into evil and disobedience.
rows.anchor: أي نذيرا لمن شاء منكم أن يتقدم إلى الخير والطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kubra is the feminine singular corresponding to kubar, like sughra/sughar and uzma/uzam; its form is built directly for the feminine, not from a masculine base.
rows.anchor: وواحدة «الكبر»، كبرى مثل الصغرى والصغر

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says people once sought shelter in mountains when frightened, but on that Day nothing will protect them from God.
rows.anchor: لا وزر يعصمكم يومئذ مني

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains that the final destination is to the Lord, paralleling the statement that the final end is to Him.
rows.anchor: إلى ربك يومئذ المستقر

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says the destination means return and recourse to God; another view says it is the afterlife where He settles and judges people.
rows.anchor: ابن مسعود: إلى ربك المصير والمرجع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading makes “no refuge; to your Lord is the destination” the person’s own words after realizing there is no escape.
rows.anchor: من قول الإنسان لنفسه إذا علم أنه ليس له مفر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن مسعود
rows.claim: The human is told what good or evil he advanced and what good or evil practice he left to continue after him.
rows.anchor: بما أسلف من عمل سيىء أو صالح، أو أخر من سنة سيئة أو صالحة يعمل بها بعده

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Nakha‘i say the person is told of his first and last deeds.
rows.anchor: منصور عن مجاهد قال: ينبأ أول عمله وآخره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas, shared by Qatada, says he advanced disobedience and delayed obedience.
rows.anchor: أي بما قدم من المعصية، وأخر من الطاعة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets the first as money spent for oneself and the later as what one leaves to heirs.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: «بما قدم» من أمواله لنفسه «وأخر»: خلف للورثة

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says it means duties performed and duties left for later.
rows.anchor: بما قدم من فرض، وأخر من فرض

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri says the disclosure occurs at the Resurrection when deeds are weighed, though it could occur at death.
rows.anchor: وهذا الإنباء يكون في القيامة عند وزن الأعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi prefers disclosure at the weighing of deeds, citing reports that good works continue to accrue after death.
rows.anchor: والأول أظهر لما خرجه ابن ماجه في سننه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra lists knowledge taught, a good child, a copied Quran, a mosque, a travelers’ shelter, a water channel, and charity as benefits that continue after death.
rows.anchor: علما علمه ونشره، وولدا صالحا تركه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “after his death while in his grave” shows that the full disclosure is not at death but at the weighing in the afterlife, although he may receive good news in the grave.
rows.anchor: نص على أن ذلك لا يكون عند الموت، وإنما يخبر بجميع ذلك عند وزن عمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later burdens others bear include the burdens of those misled without knowledge, supporting disclosure after deeds are weighed.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يكون إلا في الآخرة بعد وزن الأعمال

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report in Sahih says whoever starts a good practice receives its reward and the reward of later practitioners, while whoever starts an evil practice bears its sin and theirs.
rows.anchor: من سن في الإسلام سنة حسنة كان له أجرها وأجر من عمل بها بعده

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: These grammarians take hal as qad; al-Farra says it may mark denial or a report, and here it is a report, while another view treats it as a question meaning “it came.”
rows.anchor: بمعنى قد قاله الكسائي والفراء وأبو عبيدة

rows.speaker: قتادة والثوري وعكرمة والسدي
rows.claim: They identify the human in the verse as Adam, a view also transmitted from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: والإنسان هنا آدم عليه السلام قاله قتادة والثوري وعكرمة والسدي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Adam lay between Mecca and Taif for forty years before the spirit was breathed into him.
rows.anchor: أربعون سنة مرت به، قبل أن ينفخ فيه الروح، وهو ملقى بين مكة والطائف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report gives forty years each as clay, dark mud, and shaped clay, completing Adam after 120 years; Ibn Masud adds forty years as earth, totaling 160.
rows.anchor: وزاد ابن مسعود فقال: أقام وهو من تراب أربعين سنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says the period’s length is unknown.
rows.anchor: الحين المذكور ها هنا: لا يعرف مقداره عن ابن عباس أيضا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits from Ibn Abbas that “not remembered” means Adam was neither in heaven nor on earth.
rows.anchor: لا في السماء ولا في الأرض

rows.speaker: الفراء وقطرب وثعلب
rows.claim: They say Adam was an unrecognized shaped body of earth and clay until the spirit entered him, after which he became known and remembered.
rows.anchor: كان جسدا مصورا ترابا وطينا، لا يذكر ولا يعرف، ولا يدرى ما اسمه

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Sallam says Adam was not remembered among creation, although he was remembered by God.
rows.anchor: لم يكن شيئا مذكورا في الخلق وإن كان عند الله شيئا مذكورا

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes remembrance as rank and honor, which Adam gained when God made him a vicegerent and entrusted him with what the heavens and mountains declined.
rows.anchor: بل هذا الذكر بمعنى الخطر والشرف والقدر

rows.speaker: محمد بن الجهم عن الفراء
rows.claim: Ibn Jahm transmits al-Farra’s view that Adam existed but was not yet remembered.
rows.anchor: قال: كان شيئا ولم يكن مذكورا

rows.speaker: قتادة ومقاتل
rows.claim: Some take the negation literally: Adam did not yet exist or have a name among creatures; Qatada says humanity was created recently and no creature came after it.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: إنما خلق الإنسان حديثا ما نعلم من خليقة الله

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil proposes reordered syntax: a period passed when the human was unremembered because humanity was created after all animals and no animal afterward.
rows.anchor: في الكلام تقديم وتأخير، وتقديره: هل أتى حين من الدهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view means Adam’s descendants and the nine months of pregnancy, when the embryo is an insignificant clot and morsel.
rows.anchor: عني به الجنس من ذرية آدم، وأن الحين تسعة أشهر

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abu Bakr wished the period before Adam was remembered had continued, so people would not be born and tested.
rows.anchor: لما قرأ هذه الآية: ليتها تمت فلا نبتلى

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar likewise heard someone recite the verse and said, “If only it had finished.”
rows.anchor: وسمع عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه رجلا يقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human created is Adam’s descendant; nutfa is dripping semen, and by extension any small amount of water held in a vessel.
rows.anchor: أي ابن آدم من غير خلاف

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن رواحة
rows.claim: Ibn Rawaha’s poem uses nutfa for a small amount of fluid in a waterskin.
rows.anchor: مالي أراك تكرهين الجنه هل أنت إلا نطفة في شنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Amshaj means mixed fluids; its singular forms include mashj and mashij, and a cited line by Ru’ba witnesses to the word.
rows.anchor: واحدها: مشج ومشيج، مثل خدن وخدين

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad gives mashij as the singular and says the mixture here is semen with blood.
rows.anchor: واحد الأمشاج: مشيج يقال: مشج يمشج: إذا خلط

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra identifies the mixture as the man’s and woman’s fluids, blood, and the clot.
rows.anchor: أمشاج: أخلاط ماء الرجل وماء المرأة، والدم والعلقة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says amshaj describes red mixed with white, an explanation many language scholars prefer.
rows.anchor: الأمشاج: الحمرة في البياض، والبياض في الحمرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report says the man’s thick white fluid and woman’s thin yellow fluid combine; sinew, bone, and strength come from the man, while flesh, blood, and hair come from the woman; this is also reported as Prophetic.
rows.anchor: فما كان من عصب وعظم وقوة فهو من ماء الرجل، وما كان من لحم ودم وشعر فهو من ماء المرأة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says amshaj refers to the veins of the embryo, and also identifies it as the two colored male and female fluids.
rows.anchor: أمشاجها عروق المضغة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the man’s semen is white and the woman’s is green or yellow.
rows.anchor: نطفة الرجل بيضاء ونطفة المرأة خضراء وصفراء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: They describe human creation in stages from dust and reproductive fluid through clot, morsel, bone, and flesh, paralleling al-Mu’minun.
rows.anchor: ثم علقة ثم مضغة ثم عظم ثم لحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poem shows that wa- or aw may carry the sense of “nor”; another view identifies the sinner as a hypocrite and the ingrate as an open disbeliever, close to al-Farra’s reading.
rows.anchor: أراد ولا وجد شيخ. وقيل: الآثم المنافق، والكفور الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God morning and evening means praying at the start and end of the day: dawn, then noon and afternoon prayers.
rows.anchor: أي صل لربك أول النهار وآخره، ففي أوله صلاة الصبح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bowing at night refers to the sunset and late evening prayers; prolonged night glorification means voluntary night worship, a view Qurtubi finds sound.
rows.anchor: يعني صلاة المغرب والعشاء الآخرة

rows.speaker: ابن حبيب
rows.claim: Ibn Habib says prolonged night glorification means voluntary worship at night.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن جبيب. وقال ابن عباس وسفيان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وسفيان
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Sufyan say every occurrence of glorification in the Quran means prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وسفيان كل تسبيح في القرآن فهو صلاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, glorification may mean unrestricted remembrance, whether during prayer or outside it.
rows.anchor: هو الذكر المطلق سواء كان في الصلاة أو في غيرها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and others say the command to glorify God through a long night was abrogated by the five prayers; other views call it recommended or specific to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد وغيره: إن قوله: { وسبحه ليلا طويلا } منسوخ بالصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asil has the plurals asa’il and usul; min is partitive with a time expression, as in the verse under Nuh.
rows.anchor: على الظرف للتبعيض، كما دخلت على المفعول

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says night is clothing because darkness covers and envelops people.
rows.anchor: أي تلبسكم ظلمته وتغشاكم قاله الطبري

rows.speaker: ابن جبير والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi say night was made a time of rest.
rows.anchor: ابن جبير والسدي: أي سكنا لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Day is a time for earning a living; ma‘ash may be a time noun parallel to the preceding phrase, or a verbal noun meaning life with an omitted genitive.
rows.anchor: أي وقت معاش، أي متصرفا لطلب المعاش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven strong structures are seven heavens, firm in their construction.
rows.anchor: أي سبع سموات محكمات أي محكمة الخلق وثيقة البنيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blazing lamp is the sun; ja‘ala means created here, and wahhaj describes intense radiance.
rows.anchor: أي وقادا وهي الشمس. وجعل هنا بمعنى خلق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the sun as luminous and gleaming.
rows.anchor: وهاجا منيرا متلألئا

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة وابن عباس
rows.claim: They explain mu‘sirat as winds that compress the clouds, while a second report from Ibn Abbas says it means clouds themselves.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد وقتادة: والمعصرات الرياح. وقاله ابن عباس.

rows.speaker: سفيان والربيع وأبو العالية والضحاك
rows.claim: They say mu‘sirat are clouds ready to pour rain but not yet raining, like a young woman close to menstruation.
rows.anchor: أي السحائب التي تنعصر بالماء ولما تمطر بعد، كالمرأة المعصر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada also identifies mu‘sirat as the sky; al-Nahhas says these explanations can converge because winds pollinate clouds and bring rain.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة أيضا: المعصرات السماء، النحاس: هذه الأقوال صحاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi prefers clouds, since rain is known to come from them; if rain came from winds, wind would be the more natural source.
rows.anchor: وأصح الأقوال أن المعصرات: السحاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term mu‘sir can also mean a girl nearing puberty or a cloud nearly ready to rain; linguistic explanations connect both to approaching maturity or holding water.
rows.anchor: ويقال: هي التي قاربت الحيض لأن الإعصار في الجارية كالمراهقة في الغلام

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says a mu‘sir cloud holds water and releases it little by little; related words can mean a refuge.
rows.anchor: يقال سحاب معصر أي ممسك للماء، ويعتصر منه شيء بعد شيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ikrima read “bi-l-mu‘sirat,” whereas the written codices have “min al-mu‘sirat.”
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة ابن عباس وعكرمة «وأنزلنا بالمعصرات»

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب والحسن وابن جبير وزيد بن أسلم ومقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: These authorities take “from the mu‘sirat” to mean from the heavens.
rows.anchor: مقاتل بن حيان: «من المعصرات» أي من السموات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: They explain thajjaj as pouring continuously and heavily; the word can be transitive or intransitive.
rows.anchor: صبابا متتابعا عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وغيرهما

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj glosses thajjaj as pouring, with the water understood as pouring itself.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: أي الصباب، وهو متعد

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Asked about accepted pilgrimage, the Prophet answered: raising the voice in talbiya and spilling blood through sacrifice.
rows.anchor: فالعج: رفع الصوت بالتلبية، والثج: إراقة الدماء وذبح الهدايا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says thajjaj means abundant; Qurtubi says this is the same meaning.
rows.anchor: ثجاجا كثيرا. والمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water brings forth grains such as wheat and barley and vegetation such as fodder eaten by animals.
rows.anchor: أي بذلك الماء { حبا } كالحنطة والشعير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alfaf are gardens whose branches and trees grow closely interwoven; the word has disputed singular forms or may be a plural of a plural.
rows.anchor: أي ملتفة بعضها ببعض لتشعب أغصانها

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisa‘i gives liff or luff as singular forms of alfaf; another view treats alfaf as a plural of the plural liff.
rows.anchor: وقيل: واحد الألفاف لف بالكسر، ولف بالضم

rows.speaker: الأخفش وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and Abu Ubayda offer lafif as a singular, like sharif/ashraf.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا وأبي عبيدة: لفيف كشريف وأشراف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says it would also be sound to treat alfaf as a plural of multaffah after deleting augmentative letters.
rows.anchor: ولو قيل جمع ملتفة بتقدير حذف الزوائد لكان وجيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laffa can describe a dense garden or plant, and laf’a a thick-limbed woman; the syntax may omit “we bring forth” before gardens.
rows.anchor: ونخرج به جنات ألفافا، فحذف لدلالة الكلام عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interlacing describes closely spaced garden trees whose strong branches grow near one another.
rows.anchor: ثم هذا الالتفاف والانضمام معناه أن الأشجار في البساتين تكون متقاربة، فالأغصان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Day of Decision is the appointed time and gathering for earlier and later peoples to receive promised recompense; God separates His creatures then.
rows.anchor: أي وقتا ومجمعا وميعادا للأولين والآخرين لما وعد الله من الجزاء والثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trumpet is blown for resurrection; people come to the place of presentation in communities with their leaders, or in groups and companies.
rows.anchor: أي أمما، كل أمة مع إمامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative yawman is an appositive to the first mention of “day.”
rows.anchor: ونصب يوما بدلا من اليوم الأول

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says ten groups of the Prophet’s community are gathered in transformed forms: apes, pigs, inverted, blind, deaf and mute, tongue-chewing, mutilated, fire-crucified, carrion-stinking, or tar-clad.
rows.anchor: يحشر عشرة أصناف من أمتي أشتاتا قد ميزهم الله تعالى من جماعات المسلمين

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The report identifies the transformed groups respectively as talebearers, illicit earners and tax collectors, usurers, unjust judges, self-admiring people, hypocritical scholars and preachers, harmful neighbors, informers to rulers, selfish pleasure-seekers, and the arrogant.
rows.anchor: فأما الذين على صورة القردة فالقتات من الناس يعني النمام وأما الذين على صورة الخنازير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن الضحاك والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas through al-Dahhak and Hasan say the Great Calamity is the second blast, which brings resurrection.
rows.anchor: النفخة الثانية، التي يكون معها البعث قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: Another report identifies it as the Resurrection, so named because its terror overwhelms everything else.
rows.anchor: أنها القيامة سميت بذلك لأنها تطم على كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proverb “the valley ran and overwhelmed the villages” illustrates how the calamity overwhelms all else.
rows.anchor: جرى الوادي فطم على القري

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says Arabs use tamma for an unbearable calamity, perhaps from a horse exhausting itself in a run or water filling a river.
rows.anchor: الطامة عند العرب الداهية التي لا تستطاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another derivation is from a flood that covers a well: tamma means to bury or rise over something.
rows.anchor: هي مأخوذة من طم السيل الركية أي دفنها

rows.speaker: القاسم بن الوليد الهمداني
rows.claim: Al-Qasim ibn al-Walid identifies the calamity as the moment Paradise’s people are led to Paradise and Hell’s people to Hell; Mujahid gives the same view.
rows.anchor: حين يساق أهل الجنة إلى الجنة وأهل النار إلى النار

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan says it is the hour when the people of Hell are handed over to the guards.
rows.anchor: هي الساعة التي يسلم فيها أهل النار إلى الزبانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that Day a person remembers all that he did, good or evil.
rows.anchor: أي ما عمل من خير أو شر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Hell is exposed and seen blazing by every sighted person.
rows.anchor: يكشف عنها فيراها تتلظى كل ذي بصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation limits “whoever sees” to the unbeliever, who sees the varieties of punishment; another says believers see it to appreciate God’s blessing while unbelievers burn there.
rows.anchor: المراد الكافر لأنه الذي يرى النار بما فيها من أصناف العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted answer to “when the Great Calamity comes” is that the people of Hell enter Hell and the people of Paradise enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: محذوف أي إذا جاءت الطامة دخل أهل النار النار

rows.speaker: مالك بن دينار
rows.claim: Malik ibn Dinar is reported to read the verb for Hell becoming manifest in a variant form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مالك بن دينار: «وبرزت الجحيم»

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima and others read “liman tara,” addressing Hell as the one that sees or addressing Muhammad; the intended audience is humanity.
rows.anchor: «لمن ترى» بالتاء، أي لمن تراه الجحيم، أو لمن تراه أنت يا محمد
